_readme: Hand-curated corrections applied on top of the harvested sources. Each entry must carry a `why` and, where it asserts a fact, a `source`. Keys match the `match` block against the built record; `set` fields overwrite. Keep this file small and defensible: it is the only place in the pipeline where a human overrides the open data.

corrections.why: Wikipedia files the Big Triceratops in its New South Wales table and spells the town 'Ballendean'. Ballandean is in Queensland, in the Granite Belt near Stanthorpe; the article's own neighbouring rows (Big Apple, Thulimbah) are Queensland Granite Belt entries. Corrected state and spelling.
Empty Location cell; the row's own notes place it at East Carnarvon and then on 'The Fruit Loop' road on Carnarvon's outskirts.
Sapphire is a gemfields township west of Emerald. The Wikipedia title redirects to 'Sapphire Central, Queensland', which carries no coordinates, so the town point is supplied here.

Wikipedia's Location cell reads 'Rosetown'. Larry the Lobster stands at Kingston SE on the Princes Highway; the district council's own page for the sculpture gives that location. Build year (1979) and 17 m height are confirmed by the same source.
Wikipedia leaves the Built cell empty. The 6 m fibreglass Ned Kelly at Kate's Cottage, Glenrowan was unveiled on 14 April 1992, commissioned by Rod and Chris Gerret and built by Kevin Thomas.

Wikipedia leaves the Built cell empty. The Big Oyster was opened on 30 March 1990 by NSW Premier Nick Greiner, per the NSW Government's attraction page and contemporaneous Manning River Times reporting.

The Location cell reads 'Anmatjere', a region rather than a settlement, which geocoded ~100 km north of the sculpture. The row's own notes place it at the Aileron Roadhouse on the Stuart Highway; OpenStreetMap maps the sculpture there.

Location cell reads 'Anmatjere', a region, which geocoded ~100 km north of the sculpture. The row's notes say Mark Egan added this family group to accompany his Anmatjere Man, which stands at the Aileron Roadhouse.

Was pinned on the Nullarbor Plain, ~1,200 km from where it stands. The Location cell reads 'Forrest Highway, just north of Bunbury'; the place geocoder stripped the road type and matched Forrest, Western Australia, a real locality near the South Australian border. Fergus stands beside the Forrest Highway at Eaton, just north of Bunbury, which Nominatim places at -33.3194, 115.7281. The geocoder now tries road-derived place names last, so this class of error cannot recur.

set.name: Big Banana
set.notes: Sometimes incorrectly claimed to be the first Big Thing in Australia. (The Big Scotsman in Adelaide was built over a year earlier). The Big Banana tourist complex includes a banana-themed souvenir shop, tours of the surrounding plantation and an indoor ski slope.
set.blurb: The most famous one, the Big Banana is conveniently about halfway between Sydney and Brisbane and has grown into a kitschy tourist empire with theme park rides, water slides and more. Stop by for a selfie and a banana split.

set.name: The Big Merino
set.notes: A sculpture of a merino ram, built in 1985. Goulburn and The Big Merino were bypassed by the Hume Highway in 1992, leading to a reduction in visitor numbers. On 26 May 2007, Rambo (as the Merino is locally known) was relocated by low-loader to a new home within sight of the highway.
set.blurb: One of the more impressive Big Things, this giant Merino sheep ram stands 15 meters tall and has a gift shop inside (selling merino wool products, of course), an observatory inside the head, and what are almost certainly Australia's largest testicles behind. Add in the location right off the Hume Highway and the pies at Trappers Bakery next door, and few travelers heading from Sydney to Canberra or Melbourne can escape its woolly charms.

set.name: The Big Orange Goblin
set.notes: Located in the Inner West at the heart of Sydney's "Ale Trail”, this 30-tonne beer can is also a functioning grain silo used by The Grifter Brewing Co. The towering artwork is a realistic depiction of their best-selling beer: The Grifter Pale Ale, affectionately known as "The Orange Goblin”.

set.name: The Big Trout
set.notes: (one of two in NSW)
set.blurb: Designed by Andy Lomnici, the Big Trout is located in the town of Adaminaby, near Lake Eucumbene in the Snowy Mountains. It was built from fibreglass over a steel frame, completed in 1973, and repaired and repainted in 2023.

corrections.why: Fixed location: near Lake Eucumbene in the Snowy Mountains, matching its own blurb, not on the NSW/VIC border further west. The longitude in the first save of this correction was 144.774539, a transposed digit (should be 148) that landed the pin ~350 km away; corrected to 148.774539, confirmed against OSM node 1541562525 (historic=monument, name="The Big Trout", surveyed), which sits within a few metres of it. That same OSM node had also been wrongly attached to the separate "Big Trout" record at Harrietville, VIC (id dc68ba7a63) — see that record's own correction.

Wikivoyage's own listed coordinate for this row was wrong by ~350 km: it matched OSM node 1541562525 ("The Big Trout", a surveyed monument) within a few metres — which is Adaminaby, NSW's Big Trout, not this one. Its own notes give a specific address, 10 Stony Creek Road, Harrietville VIC, which Nominatim places at -36.852035, 147.079682 — used here instead. Dropped the openstreetmap source and osmId, since that OSM node is a different, real object at a real place, not this one.

set.name: The World's Biggest Sundial
set.notes: A 25 ft sundial presented as a gift from Lemington Mine, to honour the occasion of the Australian Bicentenary. At the time of its creation, it was recognised by the Guinness Book of World Records as the world's largest sundial, and still lays claim to being the largest one-piece sundial in the Southern hemisphere.

set.notes: The wombat depicted is a northern hairy-nosed wombat, which is critically endangered. Officially named William the Hairy-Nosed Wombat, the sculpture stands in Thallon's town park on Pine Street, next to the town's ANZAC memorial.

corrections.why: Location cell only read 'Thallon ()', an empty qualifier with no town field set. Confirmed against an OpenStreetMap node explicitly tagged tourism=artwork, description='Wombat', sitting a few metres from a separately tagged historic=memorial/war_memorial node — matching reporting that places William beside Thallon's ANZAC memorial in the town park. The prior inline coordinate was already within about 15 m of this node.

Location cell and precision were town-level ('On Princes Highway between Trafalgar and Yarragon'). The row's own notes name the exact site, 'The Spud Shed' at the corner of Princes Hwy and Rankins Rd; Nominatim/OSM maps a shop node named 'Spud Shed' at that address, giving an exact point instead of the Trafalgar town centroid. Note this sculpture is sometimes wrongly associated with Thorpdale, VIC (also a well-known potato-growing town, home of the Thorpdale Potato Festival) — the actual site is the Spud Shed roadside stall between Trafalgar and Yarragon.

additions.name: The Big Root
additions.why: Named in ABC News' roundup of obscure Australian Big Things; absent from both wiki lists.
additions.notes: A polished eucalyptus tree root, estimated 250–300 years old, that grew wide rather than deep after failing to penetrate an underlying limestone shelf. Hand-polished over 12 months with a dentistry drill by the late Jack Ramsdell; displayed in a purpose-built wooden pyramid behind a local café.

additions.name: Big Blue (The Big Blue Horse)
additions.why: Named in Destination NSW's attraction listings; absent from both wiki lists.
additions.notes: A draught-horse sculpture made from blue string by sculptor Nick Adams, standing at the Hunter Warbirds Museum, Walter Pye Avenue, Scone. Built in two sections that visitors can walk between.

additions.name: The Big Snail
additions.why: Named in Tourism WA's Big Things roundup; absent from both wiki lists.
additions.notes: A snail sculpture by artist Peter Hill, installed January 2018 to mark the start of Bremer Bay's native snail trail on Wellstead Road, opposite the dive shop and hardware store.

This row came from Wikivoyage's 'Big Aboriginal Hunter' bullet, which is the same sculpture as Wikipedia's 'The Anmatjere Man', Mark Egan's 2005 figure above the Aileron Roadhouse on the Stuart Highway. Dedup missed it because the two lists name it differently and Wikivoyage gave no address. Keeping the Wikipedia row, which carries the fuller notes.
